title: Folliculitis
summary: Pustules centred on hair follicles, usually from S. aureus, shaving or occlusion. Most cases need hygiene advice and an antiseptic rather than an antibiotic, so think about other causes if it recurs.

glance.think: Small pustules, each pierced by a hair, on the beard, scalp, thighs, buttocks or axillae, often after shaving, waxing or occlusion.
glance.engine: Inflammation of the follicle opening, usually S. aureus. Pseudomonas (hot tubs), Malassezia, or irritant/occlusive causes are possible.
glance.backbone: Stop the trigger, use an antiseptic wash, and topical or oral flucloxacillin only if persistent or extensive.
glance.never_miss: Progression to boils or cellulitis, recurrent disease (carriage, diabetes) and immunosuppression.

what: Folliculitis is **inflammation of the hair follicle**, seen as small pustules or papules centred on hairs. Superficial bacterial folliculitis is usually caused by *S. aureus*.
Deeper follicular infection becomes a **boil** (furuncle). Clusters form a **carbuncle**. See [Boils & carbuncles](condition:boils-carbuncles).

list: Follicular occlusion or damage from **shaving, waxing, tight clothing, oils**, sweating and friction.
Bacterial proliferation in the follicle opening, usually *S. aureus*. Nasal carriage drives recurrence.
Topical steroids and immunosuppression increase risk.

head: Type
Clue
Pathway
rows: 1–2 days after a hot tub or spa; under swimwear
Itchy, uniform papules on the upper back and chest; young adults; after antibiotics
Ingrown hairs in curly beard hair after close shaving

list: **Follicular-centred pustules**, often with a hair visible in the centre, on a red base.
Sites: scalp, beard (sycosis barbae), trunk, buttocks, thighs and axillae.
Itchy or tender. Systemic upset is unusual.
Clinical. The distribution and history (shaving, hot tub, recent antibiotics) point to the type.
**Swab a pustule** for culture if persistent, recurrent, extensive or atypical.
Consider a **nasal swab** for *S. aureus* carriage in recurrent disease.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Comedones present; face, chest and back; mixed lesion types
Heat and occlusion; tiny pustules not centred on follicles
Satellite pustules around a red, moist fold
Rough follicular papules on the upper arms and thighs; not pustular

list: Stop or modify the trigger: change shaving technique (a clean sharp blade, shave with the grain, or a pause in shaving), use loose clothing, and avoid oils and occlusion.
Use an **antiseptic wash** (e.g. chlorhexidine or a benzoyl peroxide wash).
Topical antiseptic or antibiotic in line with local guidance, for short courses.
Oral **flucloxacillin** if extensive (clarithromycin if penicillin allergy).

management: Swab, consider decolonisation (via the local pathway), and screen for diabetes. Think about other causes such as Pityrosporum or Gram-negative folliculitis.
red_flags: Progression to **boils, carbuncles or cellulitis**, or fever.
Recurrent disease despite measures: consider carriage, PVL or MRSA, diabetes and immunosuppression.
Widespread itchy folliculitis in an immunosuppressed patient (eosinophilic): refer.
pearls: **Pustules on the upper back and chest after antibiotics?** Think Pityrosporum folliculitis, which needs an antifungal.
A hot-tub history explains a sudden ‘swimsuit-distribution’ rash.
Most mild bacterial folliculitis settles without antibiotics, which is a useful stewardship opportunity.
Pseudofolliculitis barbae is common in curly hair. Discuss shaving technique and beard growth sensitively.
